Methodological Context & Scope The current implementation of Purple Python (PP15/PP10.py) and its predecessor QuackSink (QS 9.7) relies on Python-driven DevTools/Puppeteer protocol calls sending direct DOM querying and clicking actions into web frontends (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini). To analyze where selector fragile points occur, we evaluated three open-source automation projects: chatgpt.js (v4.15+) – Native DOM-injectable library tailored specifically to OpenAI's Web UI. multi-llm-web-orchestrator – Chrome Extension content-script bridge operating across multiple LLM web interfaces simultaneously. ai-ensemble-extension – Multi-tab LLM orchestrator leveraging browser-level message passing. Below is the comparative breakdown of the 6 core operational phases under the strict [A] / [B] / [C] evidence model: [A] = Demonstrably implemented in an existing inspected project repository. [B] = A reasonable engineering deduction derived directly from technical evidence. [C] = Analytical speculation / unverified conjecture. 1. SEND (Composer Identification & Triggering) Findings & Evidence PP15 Approach: Uses generalized, top-down fallback cascading arrays of CSS selectors (e.g., #prompt-textarea, textarea, div[contenteditable="true"]). It fills text, dispatches synthetic input events via CDP, and queries multi-candidate selector lists to click the submit button. External Implementations [A]: chatgpt.js [A]: Avoids top-down global searching by targeting known stable root wrapper IDs (#prompt-textarea or form textarea) and executing native JS prototype setter calls: Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(window.HTMLTextAreaElement.prototype, 'value').set.call(el, text). To trigger the UI state change, it dispatches an explicit new Event('input', { bubbles: true }) directly on the input element before programmatically triggering the form submission event or dispatching a KeyboardEvent (Enter with keyCode: 13). multi-llm-web-orchestrator [A]: Uses provider-specific explicit entry paths instead of guessing. Each provider has a designated input handler function (e.g., sendChatGPT(prompt), sendClaude(prompt)). For rich-text editable contenteditable divs (like Claude/Gemini), it creates text nodes (document.createTextNode(prompt)), attaches them inside paragraph

tags, and fires explicit React/ProseMirror internal event sequences (InputEvent('beforeinput'), InputEvent('input')). Structural Insights [B] Generic CSS selector loops fail in modern frontends (React, ProseMirror, Draft.js) because modifying .value or .innerText without firing native framework event hooks leaves internal virtual DOM state out-of-sync [B]. Provider-specific key-down/input emulation is cleaner than broad selector fallback lists because React/ProseMirror trees often contain hidden or clone textareas used for height calculation or hidden forms [B]. 2. BUSY / DONE (Generation State Transitions) Findings & Evidence PP15 Approach: Checks for state changes by probing action buttons (e.g., looking for "Stop generating" or aria-label="Stop" vs. send button presence). External Implementations [A]: chatgpt.js [A]: Evaluates generation state through a multi-layered check (isTyping() / isIdle()): Stop Button Observation: Queries whether an active stop button exists in the DOM ([data-testid="stop-button"], button[aria-label*="Stop"]). Streaming Cursor Detection: Queries whether an active streaming cursor element exists in the DOM (.result-streaming, .cursor, [class*="streaming"]). MutationObserver Tracking: Listens for node additions/removals directly on the active chat container rather than continuously polling DOM selectors from python over the protocol wire. multi-llm-web-orchestrator [A]: Employs explicit interval polling (setInterval) inside the browser context, checking for provider-specific DOM attributes that mark generation completion (e.g., waiting for the stop button element to vanish or the disabled state on the input box to flip back to false). Structural Insights [B] Relying exclusively on button attributes (like button label or icon) is prone to breaking whenever a provider changes UI labels (e.g., transitioning to "Start Voice" or changing SVG icons) [B]. Combining Button Presence + Streaming Indicator in Response Container + DOM Mutation State creates a multi-point verification signal that prevents false positives when a button temporarily unmounts/remounts during rendering [B]. 3. NEW RESPONSE (Identity, Scoping & Target Verification) Findings & Evidence PP15 Approach: Scrapes response nodes by index (e.g., fetching the last .markdown or [data-message-author-role="assistant"] element on the page). External Implementations [A]: chatgpt.js [A]: Uses explicit indexing scoped within the active discussion container: Grabs all assistant response blocks: document.querySelectorAll('[data-message-author-role="assistant"]'). Isolates the last element: const lastResponse = responses[responses.length - 1]. Verifies that the turn is fresh by comparing its raw text hash or index length against the snapshot taken prior to sending the prompt (getLastResponse()). multi-llm-web-orchestrator [A]: Takes a pre-send snapshot of the response count (N). Upon completion of generation, it explicitly extracts turn N+1, preventing collision with previous historical turns. Structural Insights [B] Index displacement occurs when providers insert hidden/system nodes or render status toasts into the response list [B]. Pre-send baseline snapshotting (recording current node count + last response ID/signature prior to dispatching SEND) is necessary to prove that a harvested response belongs to the current prompt turn [B]. 4. Separation of Concerns (Architecture vs. Monolithic Polling) Findings & Evidence PP15 Approach: Executes orchestration loop steps inside Python via CDP calls (PP10.py), bundling state checks, timeout retries, selector guessing, and DOM scraping into unified execution loops. External Implementations [A]: chatgpt.js [A]: Completely separates DOM interaction mechanics from state logic. It exposes modular methods (chatgpt.send(), chatgpt.isTyping(), chatgpt.response.getLast()). The consumer controls flow, while the library encapsulates single DOM actions. multi-llm-web-orchestrator [A]: Decouples browser messaging (background.js) from content scripting (content.js). The orchestrator issues high-level commands (SEND_PROMPT), and the provider adapter executes the isolated task and returns a clean payload. Structural Insights [B] Crossing the CDP/Puppeteer wire on every polling tick adds latency and risk of race conditions [B]. Executing isolated, stateful JavaScript modules directly within the browser context (returning clean state transitions back to Python) reduces protocol overhead and avoids timing sync issues [B]. 5. The core engine is provider-agnostic, maintaining a common message contract while dispatching to explicit per-provider drivers (chatgptAdapter, claudeAdapter, geminiAdapter). Each adapter defines its own input setup, send trigger, completion condition, and response extraction rules. Structural Insights [B] A unified state machine (IDLE → SENDING → GENERATING → HARVESTING → COMPLETE) decouples state flow from provider specifics [B]. Provider adapters should expose uniform interface methods (composer(), isGenerating(), getLatestResponse()) rather than leaking custom DOM selectors into the core orchestrator [B]. 6. Broad Global Fallback CSS Selectors Querying page-wide tags (textarea, button) via array loops. Fragile [B] — Highly vulnerable to DOM structure shifts and hidden UI elements. B. DOM MutationObserver Injections Injecting a JS script into the browser tab to watch DOM subtrees for stream completions. Robust [A/B] — Used by chatgpt.js [A]; eliminates network/protocol polling lag [B]. C. In-Browser Provider Adapters Running lightweight, provider-specific JS scripts inside the tab context, returning standardized JSON payloads to Python. Clean Architecture [A/B] — Used by multi-llm-web-orchestrator [A]; keeps main Python loop focused on orchestration rather than DOM parsing [B]. D. Network Response Interception / CDP Fetch Monitoring Monitoring HTTP/WebSocket stream chunks directly via CDP Network domain (Network.responseReceived / Network.webSocketFrameReceived). Alternative Route [B/C] — Completely bypasses DOM/CSS scraping [C], though requires maintaining endpoint/schema parsers across vendors [B]. Summary Checklist of Reconnaissance Observations Pre-Send Snapshotting [A/B]: Record existing response node counts before typing to avoid harvesting old or partial turns. In-Context Event Firing [A]: Use native React/ProseMirror event sequences (beforeinput, input, KeyboardEvent) to prevent text input drops. Multi-Signal Generation Tracking [A/B]: Combine stop button state with streaming indicators to avoid getting trapped by UI label changes (e.g., "Start Voice"). Adapter Encapsulation [A]: Isolate provider DOM selectors into dedicated adapters so selector updates don't break the global state machine. No code changes have been introduced. Before SEND, capture a turn baseline containing:
the existing assistant candidate identities or signatures
the current last-response anchor
the relevant composer/action identity
evidence of the generation-start transition
Then after DONE, resolve the response belonging to this SEND by finding either:
a candidate that did not exist in the pre-SEND baseline

a previously existing candidate whose content/signature changed as a result of this new generation

"what does it look like now?"
"what about now?"

IDLE
then SEND
then BUSY
then DONE
then TURN IDENTITY RESOLUTION
then HARVEST READY
then COMPLETE
Python/CDP then receives meaningful state information instead of constantly polling raw DOM state across the protocol boundary.
That is cleaner technically and fits the original DRS/MMRC idea of interacting state machines very well.
I also think provider-specific adapters are now clearly the right boundary.
The common PP core should understand the state machine.
Each provider adapter should understand that provider's local vocabulary and DOM representation:
composer
send action
busy signal
idle signal
assistant candidate scope
turn identity / response extraction
So the architecture becomes:
COMMON PP CORE:
IDLE -> SENDING -> GENERATING -> DONE -> RESOLVING -> COMPLETE
PROVIDER ADAPTER:
"Here is how THIS website represents those states."
That means if ChatGPT changes "Start Voice" to some different control tomorrow, we update the GPT adapter rather than performing surgery on the entire PP machine.
And I would preserve the PP15/16 experiments as historical evidence. They were not wasted work. They gave us the empirical observations that led us to this architecture.

We have not found a magic drop-in library.
We HAVE found a much better architectural pattern than selector whack-a-mole:
Stop making the core understand individual websites.
Make each website teach the core its local language.
That is what I think we should investigate next, before writing another PP version.

That is a logical question, Cozmo, and it actually hits on one of the biggest trade-offs in browser automation!
The short answer is: PP could pull the entire HTML string over the wire (using CDP calls like DOM.getOuterHTML), but doing raw HTML string parsing outside the browser breaks down quickly.
Here are the primary reasons why interacting with the living DOM directly inside the browser context works far better than parsing raw HTML in Python:
1. Modern Web Apps Don't Use Plain HTML (The Shadow DOM Problem)
Most AI chat UIs (like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini) rely heavily on Web Components, Custom Elements, and the Shadow DOM.
If you ask Chrome for the page’s top-level HTML string, Shadow DOM subtrees are completely hidden or encapsulated.
A simple raw HTML string dump will literally be missing the inside of the message bubbles, text areas, and custom controls.
Browser JavaScript running inside the tab can traverse through Shadow Roots (shadowRoot.querySelector), while static HTML snapshots miss them entirely.
2. HTML Text Lacks Live Execution Context & Event Status
Raw HTML is a static text snapshot of a single moment in time. It doesn't tell Python:
Whether an animation frame is mid-stream.
Whether a React or Webpack state variable inside JS has flipped to isStreaming: false.
Whether a button is currently receiving active mouse/touch event listeners.
To figure out if a streaming response has finished, you'd have to constantly serialize giant HTML strings over the CDP socket and diff them in Python. That creates massive CPU overhead and network noise compared to a tiny 5-line MutationObserver script running locally inside the tab.
3. CDP Performance Overhead
In CDP protocols (and Puppeteer / Playwright underneath), fetching the entire DOM tree (DOM.getDocument + DOM.getOuterHTML) is notoriously slow and memory-intensive.
Google’s own dev teams specifically recommend not pulling raw DOM trees across the CDP protocol boundary.
Instead, injecting a tiny snippet of local JavaScript via Runtime.evaluate to inspect elements inside the browser engine is orders of magnitude faster and doesn't freeze the tab.
Summary: The "Browser Observer" Analogy
Think of it like checking on popcorn in a microwave:
Inspecting Raw HTML from Python: Unplugging the microwave, taking the door off, pulling the bag out to read it, and putting it back every half-second.
The Browser Observer Prototype: Leaving the door closed, listening for the pops from inside the room, and having a small sensor ding only when 2 seconds pass with no pop.
By putting the observation logic inside the browser tab as local JS, Python doesn't have to keep asking for HTML updates. The page just tells Python: "Hey, Turn T is done streaming!"
